# Preface.

After many souls walking in the paths of the **inner life** <term>inner life: a spiritual tradition focusing on internal prayer and the soul's direct relationship with God</term> have requested to have the excellent writings of **Mr. Bertot** <note>original: "Herrn Bertot"; Jean de Bertot (1622–1681) was a French mystic and spiritual director associated with the Quietist movement</note> in the German language, and the providence of **GOD** Himself has provided the occasion and opportunity for some of Mr. Bertot’s letters to be translated into German; it has been deemed both necessary and useful to share this present extract from these writings with those who desire them. This collection is shared not according to a specific organized system, but rather in the sequence in which they have been and will continue to be translated.

# Preface.

...those who walk in these inner ways of the **Spirit** should take great care not to misuse the figures of speech in these **writings** in a carnal sense to excuse their own **hardness of heart** <term>hardness of heart: a theological term for a state of spiritual stubbornness or resistance to divine grace</term>, for by doing so they would only heap **damnation** upon themselves. For these testimonies are by no means written for such people, but rather only for the comfort, encouragement, and as a means of help for childlike, simple, and sincere **souls** who are currently enduring difficult trials and **temptations** <term>temptations: here referring to 'Anfechtungen,' or deep spiritual crises and feelings of abandonment by God</term>. These are souls who strive for the pure love of **GOD** with their whole heart, and who would much rather suffer death and every kind of martyrdom a thousand times over than consent to even the slightest sin.

However, so that the kind reader may also have some information about the **author** of these excellent testimonies, I will share here in the German language the entire preface that was placed before the four volumes.

# Preface

But whoever desires to have some particular information concerning **Mr. Bertot** <note>Jean de Bertot (1622–1681) was a French priest and a significant figure in the development of Quietism; he was a mentor to Madame Guyon</note>, will find the specifics of it in a short essay which comprises everything that could be learned about him; therefore, we attach the said essay here word-for-word, just as it was shared with us.

> “**Mr. Bertot** was born in the parish of **Coutances** in **Normandy**, and was ordained as a priest there. He was a great friend of the late **Mr. de Bernières Louvigny** <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659), a layman and mystic whose work *The Interior Christian* was highly influential in 17th-century French spirituality</note>, Treasurer of the Crown of France in **Caen**, who is so well known for his spiritual writings and who died on May 13, 1659, with the reputation of a holy man. After the death of this dear friend of his, whom he regarded as his spiritual father, Mr. Bertot applied himself to guiding souls in various **convents** <note>original: "Nonnen Clöstern"</note>. # ### In what manner souls [are led] Discourse 1.

...[find othe]r means, if they hold fast to God, as He will at times in a merciful manner grant them help through Himself; but at another time He will allow good counsel to be shared with them through persons who are found through providence <term>providence: the protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power</term> and in a quite ordinary way; and as they thus keep themselves upright upon the remaining wreckage of divine guidance, they will reach their salvation. 

Just as with a ship that founders at sea, but a person saves himself on a plank and swims with it bit by bit to land, yet with far greater effort and uncertainty than if he had landed with the ship intact. This is a true image of a soul that is at rest and in peace because it stands within the order of God; for such a soul can be compared to a person who travels along quite softly and comfortably in a ship. If, on the contrary, the soul steps out of the divine order or loses its way outside of God's working—even while persisting generally in its good will to be devoted to God and to belong to Him—then it resembles that person who saves himself on the remaining wreckage of the ship after it has gone to pieces. <note>The author uses the "shipwreck" metaphor to describe the difference between those who follow God's direct guidance (the ship) and those who, through their own errors, must struggle toward salvation using whatever "scraps" of grace they can find (the wreckage).</note>

## Of the Sanctified Rest

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

Since the child can only proceed with gentle steps, it causes the mother to adjust her own steps according to the child’s and to walk slowly.

The same occurs with souls who, although they walk with all faithfulness, nevertheless proceed only through their own effort and activity, being merely supported and guided by the hand of God—which is His Providence. For since God must accommodate Himself to the weakness of the creature <term>original: "Creatur"; here referring to the human being in their created state</term>, progress occurs with very gentle and slow steps, and one does not get very far. Yet, as long as the soul takes this Providence by the hand and follows it, it always moves forward, even if very slowly.

However, if this child refuses to hold its mother’s hand, but instead wishes to walk by itself and through its own strength according to its own inclination and pleasure, it falls. Instead of moving forward, it lingers and is delayed, which also causes the mother to be delayed. This same thing happens to the soul when it does not wish to be led by the hand of God and by His Providence.

12. # The 2nd Letter.

**Souls united in God see and serve each other in God, though they are absent from one another. To attain this life in God, one must pass through many "deaths" <note>In the Pietist and mystical tradition, "death" refers to the process of mortification, or the systematic letting go of one's ego, desires, and worldly attachments so that the soul can be reborn in God.</note>, which commonly spring from the smallest things of our station in life. How one must remain faithful therein in patience and self-loss. The necessity of transcending all things. Volume III. Letter 32.**

->I.<-

I assure you, Madam, that my soul finds you deeply in God; and although you are very distant in the body, we are nevertheless quite near to each other. I have felt no difference between your presence and your absence, departure, and distance. Souls united in this manner are and can always be together, provided they remain in the **one thing necessary** <note>original: "einigen Nothwendigen"; a reference to Luke 10:42, where Jesus tells Martha that her sister Mary has chosen the "one thing necessary" by sitting at his feet and listening, rather than being distracted by worldly chores.</note> and live within it. There they serve one another and comfort each other at the very least just as powerfully as if they were together. Physical presence serves no other purpose than to compensate, to some extent, for that deficiency when one does not dwell and is not lost in God, and thus cannot be together in Him nor speak with one another.

Be assured, therefore, Madam, that it is and always will be a great joy to me whenever I [can serve] you through my answer in something <note>The text ends here as a catchword for the next page, where the sentence likely continues "in something that may help your soul."</note>

### Seeing Oneself in God. 5th Letter.

...also how far they have advanced in this. They can see this through the experience of losing themselves in their faults and in their spiritual misery and poverty. For a soul that has found **GOD** enjoys inner purity; she enjoys the virtues and everything else that is called holiness, in the sense that she loses herself. And if she perceives any of this in herself and through herself—rather than by means of her own decay <note>original: "Verfaulung." In this mystical context, decay or decomposition refers to the spiritual process where the "self" or ego breaks down so that divine life can sprout, much like a seed in the soil.</note>—then she must certainly believe that she is indeed a soul of good will, but is by no means yet in **GOD**. It is there that her decay allows her to find **GOD** Himself; and the more she finds herself there and loses herself, the more she continues to decay.

<margin>which also remains alone</margin>

# The 7th Letter.

**The state of a soul in which the divine light begins to rise through the center. The certainty of the path of faith, which leads there through emptiness, uncertainty, and the loss of all things. The difference between souls in the "faith of light" and those in the "dark faith." God takes pleasure in the latter despite their weaknesses. Volume II. Letter 66.**

5. **God** also frequently disguises Himself because of the great **weakness** of His **creature** <note>original: "Creatur." ### Of the Divine Light, 7th Letter.
<meta>catchword: seek</meta>

...manner, an inclination to always surrender themselves, and this inclination never leaves them. # Of the Path of Nothingness — 9th Letter
<meta>catchword: detest</meta>

For when this is the case, then darkness is light; and the inner miseries, strippings <note>original: *Entblößungen* — a term for the spiritual process of being stripped of ego, intellect, and worldly attachments</note>, and abysses, in which it seems that one would lose oneself—these are the means to cover a great distance without becoming aware of it. Indeed, one sees it just as little as those sailing on the sea with a favorable wind can see that the ship is moving forward. All evil consists in this: that one always wants to see and to possess all things; and yet <margin>having it in a constant concept, says J. Böhme <note>Jakob Böhme (1575–1624) was a German mystic who taught that true spiritual knowledge comes through direct experience rather than intellectual "concepts."</note></margin> one must have nothing if one wishes to see **GOD** and enjoy Him. ### I.

Our Lord shares Himself with souls in two different ways according to His purpose. The first way is general and common, in that it is arranged according to the manner of the creature <note>This refers to the "natural" or "ordinary" way humans interact with the world and religion, using their senses, intellect, and standard religious practices.</note>, and through this, God sanctifies many souls in an exalted manner; namely, He enlightens the faculties <term>Faculties: In historical Christian psychology, these are the powers of the soul, specifically the intellect (reason), the will (desire), and the memory.</term> of their soul, and raises them more or less according to His counsel, so that they praise and glorify God through their exercise of the virtues, according to the light and love they possess. They are fruitful in good intentions, in fervor, and in holy inspirations <note>original: "heiligen Erfindungen." In this 18th-century context, "inventions" or "Erfindungen" refers to creative ways to serve God or new spiritual insights.</note>.

# The 14th Letter.

**The divine light of faith, by making the soul blind and small, leads it to divine immensity and freedom. One must be faithful in allowing oneself to be satisfied with the divine order from moment to moment, even if it seems ever so destructive. II. Volume. Letter 45.** <note>This likely refers to a collection of letters by a French mystic, such as Madame Guyon or François Fénelon, which were widely translated and circulated in German Pietist circles.</note>

->I.<-

Just as the entire happiness of life consists in being within the order of God; since in such a way one possesses the heart of God, and the soul can thereby be truly and completely satisfied: so this is the reason that I will primarily strive to speak to you <note>original: *ihnen*, the formal/plural "you" common in 18th-century correspondence</note> about your inner self, in order to help you, if I am capable of it, so that you may enter into this order of God.

2. # The 15th Letter.

->One must improve oneself, and endure oneself in peace and in surrender. Vol. II, Letter 59.<-

->I.<-

# On Faithfulness, 16th Letter

For when one finds God, one finds all and everything in Him—not in a human way, but in the divine way and in the manner of God; which says a great deal to a soul that has experience of it.

# On Divine Providence

...proceeds, all the more do they also become still, quiet, simple, and bare, until finally everything becomes light for them—not in a manner perceptible to the senses or obvious, but it becomes for them a true and certain light of the soul. In this state, they walk in safety without seeing anything, for they see all things through dependence and submission; and while they have nothing, they nevertheless possess all things through this very means. 

This is the reason that, as they gradually accustom themselves to this divestment <term>divestment: the German *Entblößung* refers to the mystical process of "stripping" the soul of its own desires, will, and intellectual certainties to rely solely on God.</term>, and to keeping nothing back for their own reassurance, they walk at all times in the light, as I have already mentioned. It is just like a person in an open field where no object <note>original: *Vorwurff*; in this context, it refers to a physical object or mental image that stands "before" the eyes and limits the field of vision.</note> sets a limit to their sight; they would see no specific thing, and yet they would be in a much greater and more widely diffused light. 

It is exactly the same with a soul that gradually allows itself to be stripped bare, so that it neither is anything, nor consists of anything, nor possesses anything, except what it has in divine providence through sheer dependence and submission. Through this means, God gives the soul all things, without it lacking anything, and without the soul making any provision or holding anything back, no matter what it might be. And in this way, the soul is led to total divestment in the naked light of faith, which—the more "naked" it is, without revealing or communicating anything specific to the senses—is all the more present in great abundance.

# The 18th Letter.

->The mystery of the Cross is revealed to those humble souls who are surrendered without reservation. Divine justice is the lot of pure love. Vol. II, Letter 64.<-

---

->1.<-

One can never reach an end when speaking of the Cross, since it is a wonderfully excellent mystery, and just as deep as Jesus Christ himself. This is the reason why, when God honors a person so much that He makes them a partaker of His Crosses <note>In this context, "Crosses" refers to the specific trials, sufferings, or spiritual burdens assigned to an individual for their purification.</note>, He thereby demonstrates His love and His intentions regarding them. Therefore, do not be frightened for God’s sake, but believe firmly and beyond all your own feelings that the executioners and persecutors at the beginning of the Church, instead of destroying it, rather established it wonderfully well. This is the hidden mystery of Jesus Christ—indeed, very much hidden from those who are humanly wise and strong in their own self-sufficiency, and revealed only to the little ones and the humble, who know how to surrender themselves without reservation in every regard.

2. Therefore, do not be troubled that they see their inner self <term>inner self: *Inwendiges*; a term used in mystical theology to describe the interior life or the "ground of the soul" where God dwells.</term> so poor, nor that it seems to them our Lord appears not to hear them, but rather to forsake them; yes, even that their own nature, when left to itself, grieves and gnaws with much secret vexation <note>original: *Verdruß*; implies a sense of spiritual frustration, bitterness, or weariness that arises when the ego is denied its usual comforts.</note>.

<summary>This letter introduces the "Mystery of the Cross," explaining that spiritual suffering and the feeling of being abandoned by God are actually signs of His favor and tools for strengthening the soul, much like persecution strengthened the early Church.</summary>

### Divine Justice, 18th Letter

...is to be loved, and conversely hardens a soul full of filth and sin. 6. Once a soul has found the footpath of divine justice, it no longer walks, but flies. And I must report to you on this matter what God gave a (*) person to know—who, having recently died, was a miracle of grace, and had for her lot and portion divine justice in a very great degree of purity; the effects of divine justice in her were also astonishing. But she told me: Mercy would go very slowly to God, because she is burdened with graces, gifts, presents, and favors from God, and thus her gait is grave and slow; but divine love is led by divine justice, continuing its way without being burdened with any of these things. <note>This suggests that while "Mercy" brings many spiritual comforts that can slow a soul down, "Justice" strips everything away, allowing the soul to move swiftly toward God without distraction.</note>

# The 20th Letter.

Knowledge of oneself through the true light. The way of nothingness is to be preferred over extraordinary graces. Vol. III, Letter 5.

---

->1.<-

It seems to me that I must reasonably believe that what [Person] N. tells you in his letter is very truthful; yet I can by no means believe that **God** approves of this outcome in all its present circumstances. I confess to you that such an inner state has never pleased me. In his process <note>Referring to his spiritual development or "case."</note>, one finds visions and extraordinary things which, in my opinion <margin><unclear>insofar as they are not intended to be means</unclear></margin>, have no taste of truth; it is not marked by **Jesus Christ**. When it is marked with this seal, one has a true knowledge of oneself, and consequently a settled loathing and a low regard for everything that comes from ourselves, in whatever state one may be. Indeed, the more the soul enters into **God** and loses itself, the greater loathing it has for itself; for then it knows itself so much more, which <margin>Reflection</margin> nevertheless causes no conscious deliberation <note>original: *Ueberlegung*; here meaning a "self-centered" or "intellectual" dwelling on the self.</note>, but rather a distancing from oneself through a loving loss of self.

[The one] raised up for the glorification of **God** lives indeed in a blessed way, yet unhappily as far as [spiritual] taste and **self-love** <term>Self-love (German: *Eigen-Liebe*): The ego's natural instinct for self-preservation, spiritual pride, and the desire for emotional satisfaction in religious practice.</term> are concerned. # The 22nd Letter.

->One must bear the experience of one's wretchedness <note>original: *Elend*. In this spiritual context, it refers to the soul's recognition of its own fallen, impoverished, and "miserable" state before God.</note> with joyfulness. Vol. III, Letter 16.<-

### 1.

I have read your note and can assure you how very true it is that the difference is quite large between seeing things with faith in a general sense, and seeing them with that same light of faith when it is mixed with our own experience. The first way makes things appear beautiful and lovely; the second way, however, lets us experience them as bitter and misshapen. In the meantime, however, the one leads to the other, and the first way is not purified and enlightened except through the second.

### 2.

One would like to see oneself as beautiful and pure at all times, and yet one is not: thus it happens that the light of faith—which shines into the **darkness of nature** <term>darkness of nature (Finsternisse der Natur): a theological term referring to the inherent spiritual blindness and corruption of the human ego, which remains hidden until revealed by divine light.</term> and discovers what we truly are—displeases us; not as if such a thing were not true, but because it is not of the character that the **inclination of nature** <note>original: *Neigung der Natur*. The natural human tendency toward self-gratification, pride, and comfort.</note> would like to have it.

It is very true that instead of taking it poorly, it should rather be a comfort to us, and we should rejoice when we see ourselves in this way,

<keywords>wretchedness, experience, faith, light of faith, darkness of nature, spiritual purification, self-knowledge</keywords>

10. Therefore it happens, when a soul fundamentally grasps this divine mystery <note>original: "Geheimniß"</note> and has been enlightened concerning it, that she cherishes such a great reverence <note>original: "Ehrfurcht"</note> for everything that happens to her in general, that she sees nothing better than this very thing to make her more pleasing and beautiful before His Divine Majesty. It is in this way that she remains presented before **GOD**, in order to receive—through the crosses and everything else that happens to her—the brushstrokes that work upon her beauty and her perfection <term>Vollkommenheit: in this mystical context, it refers to the soul being fully formed into the image of Christ.</term>; just like a painting that remains presented to the hand of a skillful painter, who applies various colors to it until he has finally finished his work and brought it to perfection.

## The 24th Letter.

Souls who possess a small germ <note>original: "Käumlein," a tiny sprout or seed-bud</note> of **Jesus Christ** within them must bear their misery in surrender, so that through their loss of self they may enter into the fullness of **God**. <note>Volume III, Letter 53</note>

->I.<-

It is very comforting to me to learn through your writing that my letter has been useful to you. I thank **GOD** for this from the bottom of my heart. Take good courage and be assured that both your internal and external miseries and faults will not only be useful to you, but will be infinitely advantageous, if you are faithful with a large heart and bold courage to pursue your complete loss <term>Verlierung: a central mystical concept referring to the "annihilation" or "losing" of the self-centered ego to make room for God</term>, your death, and the forgetting of yourself in everything that holds you back within yourself. You must continue until you no longer think of yourself at all, and concern yourself with your own self as little as with a dishcloth or with dung that is no longer useful for anything: it is precisely through this that you will be prepared to be emptied, so that **Jesus Christ** may be born in you.

<header>His Misery, 24th Letter.</header>

2. Oh, if only souls knew the great good they could acquire through their faults, their miseries, and their both internal and external wretchedness <note>original: "Armseligkeiten," referring to states of spiritual or material poverty</note> when they have the small germ <note>original: "Käumlein," a tiny sprout or seed-bud</note> of **Jesus Christ** within them; they would then make excellent use of such things—not by trying to rid themselves of them through specific, forced acts of will, but rather by rotting away and being freed from themselves through the decomposition that these miseries cause in them.

3. This mystery is for those souls who already have the small germ of **Jesus Christ** within them. For as for those souls who are still striving after **Jesus Christ**, they must remain faithful in composed peace <term>gelaßner Ruhe: a state of surrendered stillness or "Gelassenheit," a central concept in German mysticism meaning a total letting-go of the self-will</term> while they combat their faults in order to purify themselves. This is because our souls cannot approach **God** except through likeness; just as one cannot approach purity except through purity. But when, through **God's** mercy, it is time to be near **God**—and since **God** is an abyss—one cannot be with Him except by losing oneself. Now, it is certain that nothing causes us to lose ourselves, or makes us lose so much of ourselves, as our wretchedness, faults, and miseries. Therefore, **Jesus Christ** speaks these beautiful words: **Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit.** (John 12:24-25).

<vocab>Souls, Misery, Wretchedness, Small germ of Jesus Christ, Decomposition, Mystery, Composed peace, Purity, Mercy of God, Grain of wheat, John 12</vocab>

<summary>This page explores the mystical necessity of spiritual "decay," suggesting that a soul's faults and miseries are the very tools God uses to break down the ego. By comparing the soul to a grain of wheat, the author explains that true spiritual fruitfulness only comes after the self has "died" or "rotted away" to make room for Christ.</summary>

<keywords>self-loss, Gelassenheit, spiritual purification, mysticism, grain of wheat, Jesus Christ, internal misery, decomposition of the self</keywords>

<header>to bear in surrender.</header>

24. 25.) Our faults and our miseries are the manure pile <note>original: "Misthauffe"</note> that causes this grain of wheat to rot and sprout. Nevertheless, one can never learn this lesson; for it cannot be put into practice except by losing oneself.

4. Therefore, the more such a soul has wretchedness, faults, and miseries surrounding her to her very innermost core, and the more she makes good use of them—without turning back to herself to complain <margin>reflection upon oneself</margin> or to help herself in any way other than by losing herself, and thereafter, by letting herself be lost—the more blessed <note>original: "glückseliger," meaning both happy and spiritually beatified</note> such a soul is. This is because her blessedness has as few limits as her misery is great. Through this, and through this process, the entire ground <term>Grund: a central term in German mysticism referring to the "ground" or deepest essence of the soul where it meets God</term> of such a soul passes over into **God**; and she reaches the point where she has no other ground than in **God** Himself; for her wretchedness undermines her entire own ground. She becomes like those abysses in which one loses oneself without being able to find oneself again. Therefore, what constitutes the misfortune of souls who do not use it in this way becomes a source of blessedness for those other souls. Not knowing where one is, nor how one stands, and hoping for nothing, is the sum of all good, since in the sense mentioned above, one possesses nothing.

5. Thus they bear their miseries, their faults, and everything else that is within them—

### His Wretchedness – 24th Letter

Fullness of God Himself, which is just as great and expansive as the loss <note>The author uses "Verlierung" to describe the mystical loss of the ego or self-will.</note> in the face of such faults has been great. Therefore, as much as our miseries and corruptions cause us to decay—insofar as we thereby go out of ourselves—just as much do we enter into the Fullness of God, and in this Fullness and through this Fullness, we improve every misery that weighs us down. This is also the reason why those souls who have already progressed far in this process <term>Process: A technical term in Pietism and mysticism referring to the "Process of Christ," or the stages of spiritual transformation the soul undergoes.</term> allow themselves to decay through their faults in all their length and breadth, and thus have no boundaries in their loss of self; they are also not held back in the remedy of these very miseries by any reflections, nor by anything that might touch them or be seen as their own.

8. Let us conclude this subject here, for otherwise we would never reach an end. Be only faithful in not lingering on yourself: endure your miseries in peace and while losing yourself. # The 26th Letter.

**Total loss of self is necessary to possess Jesus Christ. Advice for guiding souls. Volume III. Letter 62.**

->I.<-

I leave my pen, in order to write to you, in the hand of the kind GOD, so that he may give me the moments he has destined for this purpose. I find myself quite well in this: for besides the fact that I am but a foolish beast <note>German: *dummes Thier*. A common expression of radical humility in 18th-century mystical writing, suggesting the author has no independent wisdom or intellect apart from God.</note>, such that I am unable to write anything to you or anyone else unless his divine light is present within me; I also believe that without this, I would lose everything and would mix human things with the divine in your soul. I must not pause to report news to you that comes from me, but I must give you such things from GOD; it must therefore be GOD who reveals these things to me. This is also what reassures me in everything I write to you: for it seems to me that this is in his light and in his order, so that you can hold to it without fear—that is, with certainty—even though fear might overtake you.

# On Total Abandonment, 26th Letter.

2. Consider the <term>process</term> <note>German: *Process*. # The 27th Letter.

->What the Light of the Center or of Truth is, as distinguished from the faculties. Its effects. Concerning death, loss, the recognition of one's nothingness, and surrender to Providence. <note>The citation "III. Vol. Lettr. 69" refers to the third volume of a collected edition of letters, likely those of the mystic Antoinette Bourignon or Madame Guyon.</note><-

### My very dear brother!

->I.<-

I reply to your letter with great joy, as I see your growth in the gift of God, which is truly very great, insofar as it begins to reveal to you the Light of Truth—or the Light of the Center, which is the same thing—and causes you to see it. It is called the Light of Truth because it reveals God, who is Truth itself; and in this revelation, it enables one to enjoy Him little by little. The light of the faculties <note>In 17th-century spirituality, the "faculties" refer to the powers of the soul: the intellect, the will, and the memory. The author distinguishes between human mental effort and direct divine illumination.</note>, although it is indeed true and leads the soul toward the Truth, is nevertheless not called the Light of Truth, because it never gives anything other than the particular <note>meaning specific, individual pieces of knowledge or methods</note> and the means, but not the ultimate goal—that is, God Himself.

<summary>This page concludes a report from the Canadian missions of 1673 and introduces a new letter regarding the mystical "Light of the Center," distinguishing direct divine revelation from the soul's natural mental powers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the 27th letter, which explains the distinction between the "Light of Truth" (or "Light of the Center") and the natural faculties of the human soul.</meta>

### ...and its effects.

It is also called the **Light of the Center** <note>original Latin: "Licht des Centri"</note>: because it alone can illuminate this divine part where God is and dwells; however, it is never able to illuminate the <term>faculties: The natural powers of the human soul, traditionally identified as memory, intellect, and will.</term> or powers of the soul. Instead, it causes these faculties to sink away and become powerless, and this occurs through the immeasurable expanse of such Light of the Center, which always originates from the greatness of God, in whatever small degree of beginning this light might be present in a soul. Therefore, this Light of the Center is never directed toward this or that specific thing, but is a universal light; it is also not found in multiplicity, but in **unity**. And since the faculties can never possess anything other than specific or particular light, they are unable to receive this [Light of the Center], except by vanishing—much like stars in the light of the sun—and blissfully losing themselves in the **Center**, to which this divine light leads them step by step as it increases and grows.

Take careful note of what I say: that in whatever degree of beginning the said light might be, it is nonetheless universal as well as entire and complete, since it is a radiance of the face of God. And yet, this completeness or entirety increases constantly as it gradually illuminates this center of the soul and brings forth the **eternal Truth** (or God) within this center.

**Vocabulary:** Light of the Center, Soul, Faculties, Unity, Center, Eternal Truth, GOD.

This, however, causes no small difficulty for those souls who possess some seeds of the <term>Light of the Ground: the deepest, most essential part of the soul where it meets the divine</term>. For they repeatedly believe they have found the matter and the mystery, yet they subsequently find that it is not so. This happens because the <term>faculties: the soul's natural powers, such as reason and will</term> (*) can never <margin>on their own</margin> receive anything other than created things and in a created manner; and just as creatures are in fact nothing <margin>for, or in themselves</margin>, so too everything that acts upon us or is communicated to us in a created manner is always nothing.

With the <term>Light of the Center: the direct, unmediated illumination from God at the soul's core</term>, it is entirely different. In it, one sees nothing, and yet sees everything; in it, one has everything, and yet possesses nothing; in it, one notices nothing, and yet enjoys everything. Thus, this light has nothing external nor anything glittering that deceives, and one must always judge in faith—that is, in the unknown and in the hidden. One does this when they take their rest alone as their assurance.

All created species <note>original: *Especes*; a philosophical term referring to the mental images or "types" through which we normally perceive the world.</note>, lights, acts, elevations, and the like are lost here, and where the soul is raised up to contemplate in perfect nakedness: which yet cannot properly be called contemplation;

### In the Life: Letter to Mr. Bertot

Ezekiel (Chapter 1, Verse 9) in the vision of the four beasts <note>Referring to the "living creatures" in the prophet Ezekiel's vision of the chariot of God</note> seems to be well explained. *They did not turn back as they went.* <note>original Latin: *Non revertebantur cum incederent*</note> When they moved, they did not need to turn themselves around. This is my way of preaching, speaking, and writing; and from this it also follows that I can foresee nothing. I am always full and always empty: I see nothing in myself but darkness, poverty, weakness, and misery—in a word, *Nothing*, and worse than nothing, the source <term>source</term><note>original: *Principium*; in this context, the root or starting point from which actions flow</note> of all sins. I find the exact opposite in Jesus Christ, who is all things to me.

3. The good Father Allemann died this winter; and it has not entered my thoughts to take another guide for my inner life. I would not be able to consult such a person for advice; for I am not the one who establishes or orders this interior state; it does not stand under my power or regulation, or to say it better, I have no inner life; God Himself is my inner life.

Regarding outward things, one converses with others and with the good Jesuit Fathers, according to various circumstances and needs. I believe I have described my present state to them sufficiently, from which they will be able to judge all particular effects and consequences.

### A Response to the Previous Letter.

How God becomes everything and works in the soul that has died to itself and is faithful in surrendering itself to the present moment <term>present moment</term><note>This refers to the "Sacrament of the Present Moment," a core concept in 17th-century mysticism where one finds God’s will in the immediate circumstances of life rather than in complex rituals or future plans</note>, in which it finds its purification and everything else, without being either idle or under compulsion. Volume 3, Letter 70.

### On Annihilation, 29th Letter. ###

# Concerning Annihilation, 29th Letter.
<meta>catchword: 11. Through</meta>

...should share, such a thing is impossible: for if many whole books were required to describe the state of each preceding Annihilation <term>Vernichtigung: the mystical process of the soul's ego being reduced to "nothing" so God can fill it</term> even a little, then one would have to produce infinitely many books to speak with any depth of the Annihilation just mentioned: for God, who is an infinite Being, gives Himself; and thus a Nothingness equal to His greatness is required to receive God. Therefore, one must describe what God is, and what He gives, when He gives Himself in this degree of Nothingness.

Here, the soul becomes through this nothingness in God that which a drop of water is in the sea, when it loses itself therein: for as this nothingness draws the soul out of its **own-property** <term>Eigenthum: in this context, the soul's self-centered attachment to its own will and identity</term>, which sin had imparted to it, so it also draws the soul hereby out of itself and out of the **particular** or **individual**, and thus causes it to flow into God and lose itself in Him.

<margin>Not the personality</margin>
But just as the soul loses its **Self** or its **I-ness** <term>Ichtheit: the quality of being a separate "I"; the ego-identity</term>, precisely as it loses the particular or the distinct which makes it consist in itself, and as it also finds God through this, and consists in Him through this nothingness; so it finds God not as something it might *enjoy* <note>The author distinguishes between "enjoying" God as an object and being "possessed" by God in union.</note>, but rather it is possessed by God in a total and complete possession of itself.

->**Of the Gift of Faith.**<-

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

...make a distinction between this gift of faith, which constitutes inner prayer, and the faith that makes us Christians. It is exactly the same faith, and yet it is also not exactly the same: it is the same because, truly, we received the *habitus* <term>habitus: a theological term (from the Latin "habitus") referring to an infused quality or a "spiritual seed" planted in the soul by God, making it capable of acting in a certain way.</term> or the little seed of it in **Baptism**, only that it has been reawakened through a special grace: and herein the distinction is seen. 

For this reason, it happens that those souls who are so blessed as to be enlightened by this divine gift in all three degrees—that, I say, these souls also perceive the great gift of **Baptism** excellently well. A soul that was made a Christian through **Baptism** also received the seed of everything it now enjoys through the Third Degree: therefore, it is a great comfort to the soul when it sees in the **Holy Scripture** and in the **Church Fathers** <note>The influential early Christian theologians whose writings are considered foundational to the faith.</note> what they report concerning **Baptism**, and in what manner the *habitus* or the root of faith—as well as the other gifts and especially the communion of the **Holy Trinity**—is given to our soul therein, as our soul is incorporated into **Jesus Christ**. 

Outside of direct experience, one cannot believe how much this gift of faith in this third degree contains within itself the gifts of the **Holy Spirit** and all virtues—or rather, to put it better, how faith brings it about that one finds **Jesus Christ**, the **Holy Trinity**, and in **Jesus Christ** all gifts. This is unspeakable...

# Of the Three Degrees

...and cannot be explained; however, it is very truthful, very essential, and not difficult for the one to whom God gives it, being a contemplation in the **Spirit** <note>German: *Geist*</note> of a truth of the life of **Jesus Christ**. And then one finds that the knowledge <term>German: *Wissenschafft*; here referring to "sacred science" or the formal study of theology</term> of the holy Church is very pleasant among those who have this gift and have also studied alongside it. Oh, if only the scholars, who fill their heads with much study, were humble enough to give themselves over to holy interior prayer! For when they receive this gift, oh, how wonderful their joy would be as they pass through this **Third Degree**, when they would then see revealed that which their learning only makes them stammer about crudely, so that they have neither eyes nor ears to see and hear it! But let us set this aside: the joy consists in enjoying it without worrying about the rest, except that one wishes to lose oneself without finding oneself again, once one has it.

10. According to my thoughts—which I nevertheless submit in all things <note>A standard formula of the era where a writer submits their private revelations or opinions to the judgment of the Church.</note>—they should always ground themselves upon a foundation, which is that God demands and desires from them that they should prefer their relief <note>German: *Erleichterung*; likely referring to spiritual ease, unburdening, or divine illumination granted in prayer</note> over many intentions and insights they might have regarding the community and might believe it only right that they should have them. This being presupposed, I do not believe that they should do what they are telling me, especially since it is a much greater and more general advantage and blessing...

1. It is a great perfection to rob God of nothing, to refuse God nothing, and to desire nothing from God. <note>This reflects the "disinterested love" central to Quietist spirituality—loving God for Himself, not for His gifts.</note>

### of Father la Combe.

9. Who has been able to grasp how far the sovereign homage <term>German: *Homagia*; from the Latin *homagium*, referring to the formal allegiance a vassal owes to a lord. Here it signifies the soul's total submission to God.</term> extends, which one is obligated to pay to the will of God?

10. The simplicity of the dove <note>A reference to Matthew 10:16: "Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves."</note> consists in not judging, and the wisdom of the serpent consists in this: that one should distrust oneself.

11. The door through which the soul departs from its peace is the seeking of itself and its own interests; and the door through which it enters this peace again is its total and complete surrender <term>German: *Uebergabe*; a key concept in Quietism referring to the passive yielding of the self to the divine.</term> into the hands of God.

12. Ah, how hard and painful it is when one desires nothing but the will of God, and yet believes they have done nothing other than what is contrary to this divine will! How hard it is to wish for nothing so much as to fulfill this will of God, and yet not even be able to recognize it! How bitter it is when one can point out this will of God to others with complete certainty, and yet cannot find it for oneself! When one is entirely filled and permeated by it, one no longer recognizes it. <note>This describes a state of "pure faith" where the soul is so united with God's will that it loses the ability to perceive its own virtue or standing.</note> This is a long and severe martyrdom; yet it is such a martyrdom that is meant to give birth to an unchangeable and indestructible peace in this life, and an incomprehensible blessedness in the life to come!

13. Whoever has learned to seek nothing but the will of God always finds what they are seeking.

### Wise Sayings of Father la Combe.

14. Which of the two would a perfect lover choose, if given the choice: to love God, or to be loved by God?

15. God is infinitely more glorified through the sacrifices of death than through the sacrifices of life: through the latter, one treats Him as a great monarch; but through the former, one behaves toward Him truly as toward a God, in that one loses everything to glorify Him. Therefore, Jesus Christ also performed far more sacrifices of death than sacrifices of life; and I believe no one will gain everything unless <margin><unclear>and so life is one's own</unclear></margin> they have first lost everything; just as the final step to being in [true] life is the loss of all life. This final stroke of Purgatory (or cleansing) <term>German: *Fegfeuer* or *Reinigung*. 16. Reason must not desire to grasp the most extreme losses; because these are ordained to ensure that we lose this very reason <note>In mystical theology, the "loss of reason" refers to moving beyond intellectual understanding into a direct, wordless experience of the Divine.</note>.

<margin>just as one cannot [stand] before his master, so one cannot <unclear>stand</unclear> before his own desire</margin> 17. O Lord, you who search the hearts, you see whether I expected anything of myself, or whether I wished to refuse you anything!

18. How rare it is that a soul departs from all its own interests, to enter solely and uniquely into the interest of God!

19. Be just as great an enemy to yourself as you desire to be a friend of God.

However, he will only give up the Wolfersdorf Forest (if he still owns it), because the Lamberg Forest on the Ochsenberg is already mortgaged and has been handed over to Jewish businessmen for exploitation by means of a glass factory.

The Wolfersdorf Forest measures 3,000 <term>Tagwerk<note>A historical unit of land area representing what one man could plow in one day, roughly equivalent to 0.8 acres.</note></term> and is poorly stocked with trees.

Franz Baader will demand at least 30 florins, and I do not even believe that he will grant a two-thirds <term>Schonung<note>In forestry, this refers to a protected area where young trees are allowed to grow without being harvested.</note></term>.
